newsitem.title: USA: Reader's profits drop, to invest in publishing, promotion.
newsitem.headline: Reader's profits drop, to invest in publishing, promotion.

text.p: Reader's Digest Association Inc. Wednesday reported a sharp drop in earnings for the latest quarter and set plans to spend up to $400 million to boost its business, but its stock sank as investors remained skeptical.

The publisher and direct marketer of magazines, books, music, videos and new media products said net income fell 33 percent to $37.6 million, or 35 cents a share, in its third fiscal quarter ended March 31 from $55.8 million, or 51 cents a share, a year earlier.

The company's stock touched a 12-month low of $23.50 as industry analysts said the planned investment would not address slumping revenues that have plagued the Pleasantville, N.Y.-based company. The shares closed down $2.50 at $23.75 on the New York Stock Exchange.
"This is not a special program," Josephthal Lyon & Ross analyst Dennis McAlpine said. "This is just saying, 'our costs are going up.'"
Revenues fell 8 percent to $684.3 million from $747.5 million, as higher circulation in the Pacific and other markets were offset by decreases in Europe and the United States.
Lower revenues, increased promotion spending and investments in new countries reduced operating profit significantly, the company said.

With the investment initiative, the company said, it expects earnings next year to decline as it begins to stabilize and build its customer base, produce growth and maximize the value of its global franchise.
The initiatives include identifying consumer interests, retaining existing customers, tapping into new and younger customers and making selective price reductions.
"There's a concern that the money's not going to be effective," Argus Research analyst John Eade said. "It's a confidence issue. Investors don't have confidence in Reader's Digest management."

Analysts said Reader's Digest has made some strategic missteps, including oversaturating the European market with direct mail and not filling some orders after restructuring cutbacks about a year ago.
"They kind of burned out their customers" with too many mailings offering too many products in too short a time, Edward Jones analyst Linda Bannister said.
It said it expects to record one-time charges in the fourth quarter of up to $100 million.
For the third quarter, revenue at Reader's Digest magazine dropped 1 percent, books and home entertainment products fell 11 percent and special interest magazines slid 22 percent.
"This is what used to be a 15 percent grower with cash in the bank that has changed dramatically," McAlpine said. "They've made a number of wrong assumptions."

Bannister said the company sought to outline its strategy in a call with analysts on Wednesday. "But they didn't really give any detail," she said. "They're making strikes in the right direction. But no one really knows what exactly is going to work. ... No one really knows when this is going to turn."
